#### Fact 6.1.2.

The smooth open set $\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ containing ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ , is an open subset of $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ and satisfies

$$ \displaystyle U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\setminus\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times(0,1], $$

with $\Lambda$ a smooth diffeomorphism such that

$$ \displaystyle\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big) \displaystyle\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times\{0\}, \displaystyle\partial\big(\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big) \displaystyle\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times\{1\}. $$

The reader should now consult Figure 3 for intuition.

### 6.2. Calibrating $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$

In this subsection, we will show how from our construction of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ , we naturally get a smooth metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ defined throughout $M$ such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated by a smooth form $\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ defined on $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right).$

We need the following classical fact.

#### Fact 6.2.1.

The closed smooth form $\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}}^{\ast}\phi_{C}\wedge\pi_{S^{s}}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{S^{s}}$ calibrates $C\times S^{s}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ with the product Riemannian metric of standard metrics on the two factors.

Here $\phi_{C}$ is the smooth form calibrating $C$ , defined in Assumption 4.2.1, and $\operatorname{dvol}_{S^{s}}$ is the volume form of $S^{s}$ , $\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}}$ and $\pi_{S^{s}}$ are projections onto the $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ and $S^{s}$ factors, respectively, in the product $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$ The above fact follows directly from [25, Chapter II, Proposition 7.10], which says that the wedge product of a calibration form $\psi$ and a unit simple form remains a calibration in the product metrics, and calibrates precisely the product of calibrated submanifolds of $\psi$ and the submanifolds with tangent spaces dual to the unit simple form.

Now, using Lemma 4.1.3 we see that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated in $U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ by a smooth form

$$ \phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,=\Gamma^{\ast}(\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}}^{\ast}\phi_{C}\wedge\pi_{S^{s}}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{S^{s}}) $$

in a smooth metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ that is the pullback of the standard product metric on $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ under $\Gamma$ . By Fact 3.1.4, $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated in $U(N\cap N)$ by a smooth form in a smooth metric.

Recall Definition 6.1. Now we can sum up the construction in this section:

#### Fact 6.2.2.

We have a smooth Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ and a smooth form $\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ on $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated in $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ by $\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ with respect to $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,.$

Now extend $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ on $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ to a smooth Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ defined throughout $M.$

### 6.3. Calibrating the regular set of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$

In this subsection, we want to calibrate the regular set of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in a smooth metric. A natural idea pioneered in [59] is to use the pullback of the volume form of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ under the normal bundle exponential map of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a calibration form in a renormalized metric. Unfortunately, ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is an open manifold with limit points in ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ Thus, we have to go through a more complicated route by restricting to a compact subset of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ and taking into account that we have to make space for gluing of calibrations in the next subsection.

Let us first discuss what compact subsets of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ we want to deal with. Write

$$ \displaystyle\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=({\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right))\cap\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)^{\complement}. $$

By transversality, we can assume that $\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ is a smooth submanifold with boundary.

Let $\exp^{\perp}$ be the exponential map from the normal bundle $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ to $M.$ Here $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}$ means the normal bundle of a submanifold with respect to the ambient manifold $M.$ Without loss of generality, we can assume that $\exp^{\perp}$ is a diffeomorphism when restricted to the following ball bundle

$$ \displaystyle B^{\perp}_{\delta}\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=\{(p,v)\,|\,p\in\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)),\textnormal{ }v\in\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right),\textnormal{ }h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(v,v)\leq\delta^{2}\}, $$

over the base $\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$

The image of $B^{\perp}_{\delta}\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ under $\exp^{\perp}$ is a set of points with distance at most $\delta$ to $\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . Write

$$ \displaystyle B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))=\exp^{\perp}B^{\perp}_{\delta}\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)). $$

Without loss of generality, we can assume that

$$ \displaystyle\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)^{\complement}\cap U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\subset B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))). $$

See Figure 3 to get an intuition. This seemingly odd (6.2) is to prepare for the gluing of calibrations in the next subsection.

Let $\widecheck{\pi}$ denote the projection onto base $\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ in the ball bundle $B_{\delta}^{\perp}\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$ Then on $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))$ , define

$$ \displaystyle{\pi}=\widecheck{\pi}\circ(\exp^{\perp})^{-1}. $$

In other words ${\pi}$ is the nearest distance projection of $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))$ onto $\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$ The projection ${\pi}$ provides a smooth orthogonal splitting of the tangent spaces to $M$ in $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))$ into

$$ \displaystyle\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi\oplus\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi. $$

Here $\oplus$ is the Riemannian direct sum of vector spaces, and $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ is the orthogonal complement of $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi.$ By definition of $\pi,$ $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ are tangent spaces to the level sets of $\pi,$ i.e., the submanifolds formed by geodesics orthogonal to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ Thus, $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ restricted to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is the tangent space to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ . Heuristically, one should think of $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ as the natural extension of the tangent space of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ into the ball bundle.

This also provides a natural smooth splitting of the Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ into

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,=(h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,)|_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus(h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,)|_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}. $$

Here $\oplus$ means the Riemannian sum of the metrics on orthogonal subspaces.

In $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))$ the pullback of the volume form $\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}$ of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ under $\pi$ , i.e.,

$$ {\pi}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}), $$

is a closed simple form, because the form $\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}$ is a closed simple $d$ -form and consequently its pullback under the projection ${\pi}$ is also closed and simple. With respect to the splitting (6.3), the form ${\pi}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)})$ can be written as

$$ \displaystyle{\pi}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)})=\big({\pi}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)})(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)\big)\big(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi\big)^{\ast}. $$

Here $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ also denotes the unit simple $d$ -vector representing $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ and $(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\ast}$ denotes the unit simple $d$ -form Riemannian dual to the unit simple $d$ -vector $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi.$ Then we have the following fact:

#### Fact 6.3.1.

The smooth closed form

$$ \phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}={\pi}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}) $$

is a calibration form defined on

$$ B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))) $$

that calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))$ , with respect to the metric

$$ h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}=(\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi))^{\frac{2}{d}}h_{{\operatorname{Sing}}\,}. $$

The above fact is taken from [58, Remark 3.5]. The proof is a simple calculation using definition of comass, i.e., bullet (2) of Fact 2.9.1.

### 6.4. Calibrating $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ by gluing calibrations

Now we have come to the crux of the matter. We will glue the metrics and calibrations we have obtained so far to make $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ area-minimizing in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$ This subsection is taken from the proof of [58, Theorem 4.6].

By equation (6.2), Fact 6.3.1 and Fact 6.2.2, in the region

$$ \displaystyle\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\setminus\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\cap U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)), $$

we have two Riemannian metrics $h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,},h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ and two smooth calibrations forms $\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,},\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ , so that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated in this region by the corresponding forms in the corresponding metrics, respectively. Now our goal is to glue these pairs of Riemannian metrics and calibration forms together. The gluing is based on the following central fact:

#### Fact 6.4.1.

Let $g$ be a positive definite quadratic form on $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ , $\psi$ be a constant $d$ -form on $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}=P\oplus Q$ be a direct sum decomposition of $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ into orthogonal complementary subspaces $P$ of dimension $d$ and $Q$ of dimension $c$ with respect to $g$ , such that $\psi(P)>0.$ Then in the metric

$$ \displaystyle h=(\psi(P))^{\frac{2}{d}}\big(g|_{P}\oplus(Kg|_{Q})\big), $$

$\psi$ has comass

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{comass}_{h}\psi=1, $$

and calibrates $P,$ provided the real number $K$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle K\geq\binom{d+c}{d}(\psi(P))^{-1}\operatorname{comass}_{g}\psi. $$

Here $\psi(P)$ mean the value of $\psi$ at the simple unit $d$ -vector representing $P$ with respect to $g.$ The above fact is just a restatement of [58, Lemma 3.4, Remark 3.5], which is in turn a restatement of a classical result on comass by Harvey-Lawson [24, Lemma 2.14].

Roughly speaking, in the glued calibrations, the only component that matters to us is $\psi(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\ast}.$ Then Fact 6.4.1 will enable us to basically annihilate the effects of other terms spanned by covectors in $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi^{\ast}$ in the glued calibration form.

#### 6.4.1. Notation convention

From now on, we will restrict our attention to the region $\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\setminus\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\cap U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . We adopt the notation:

$$ \displaystyle U_{\operatorname{gluing}}=\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\setminus\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\cap U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)). $$

Recall that $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ is defined throughout $M$ and $h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ is obtained by rescaling $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ (Fact 6.3.1).

Thus, from now on, we will use $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ as our base metric and use the symbols

$$ \displaystyle h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}= \displaystyle(h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,)|_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}, \displaystyle h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}= \displaystyle(h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,)|_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}. $$

Then by definition we have

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,=h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}. $$

#### 6.4.2. Anti-derivatives of forms

By Lemma 4.1.3, $U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ deformation retracts onto ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C).$ On the other hand, by Assumption 5.4.1, $U(N\cap N)$ deformation retracts onto $N\cap N.$ Thus, $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ deformation retracts onto ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ Since ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is a subcomplex of dimension less than $d,$ we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle H_{d}(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right),\mathbb{Z})=0. $$

By the universal coefficient theorem [27, Theorem 3.2], this implies that

$$ \displaystyle H^{d}(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right),\mathbb{R})=0. $$

By De Rham’s theorem for smooth manifolds with boundary [45, Theorem 2.48], we deduce that there is a smooth $(d-1)$ -form $\Phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ on $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ such that

$$ \displaystyle d\Phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,=\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,. $$

On the other hand, by transversality, we can assume that $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is a smooth $d$ -dimensional manifold with boundary, thus

$$ \displaystyle H_{d}(U_{\operatorname{gluing}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right),\mathbb{Z})=0. $$

Again, by the universal coefficient theorem and De Rham’s theorem for manifolds with boundary, we deduce that $\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}$ is exact on $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ . Since $\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ is the pullback of $\operatorname{dvol}_{N\#\sigma^{s}(C)}$ under $\pi,$ we deduce that there is a smooth- $(d-1)$ form $\Phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ on $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle d\Phi_{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}=\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}. $$

#### 6.4.3. Dividing $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ into four regions

By Fact 6.1.2, we have

$$ \displaystyle U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\setminus\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right) \displaystyle\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times(0,1], \displaystyle\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big) \displaystyle\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times\{0\}, \displaystyle\partial\big(\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big) \displaystyle\overset{\Lambda}{\cong}\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times\{1\}. $$

Let $\rho$ be the smooth function defined by

$$ \displaystyle\rho=\pi_{(0,1]}\circ\Lambda. $$

Here $\pi_{(0,1]}$ is the projection onto the $(0,1]$ factor of $\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times(0,1].$

*Figure 4. Gluing of forms and the change of metrics*

#### Definition 6.4.2.

For any interval $(a,b)\subset(0,1]$ , define

$$ \displaystyle U_{(a,b)}=\rho^{-1}(a,b)\cap U_{\operatorname{gluing}}. $$

We will single out four regions of $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})} \displaystyle=\rho^{-1}\bigg(0,\frac{1}{3}\bigg)\cap U_{\operatorname{gluing}}, \displaystyle U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})} \displaystyle=\rho^{-1}\bigg(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}\bigg)\cap U_{\operatorname{gluing}}, \displaystyle U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})} \displaystyle=\rho^{-1}\bigg(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6}\bigg)\cap U_{\operatorname{gluing}}, \displaystyle U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)} \displaystyle=\rho^{-1}\bigg(\frac{5}{6},1\bigg)\cap U_{\operatorname{gluing}}. $$

The reader should now consult Figures 3 and 4 for intuition.

#### 6.4.4. Auxiliary functions

Let $\alpha:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth monotonic function that is $0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $1$ on $[1,\infty)$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{0}= \displaystyle\alpha\circ(3{\rho}{}), \displaystyle\lambda= \displaystyle\alpha\circ(3\rho-1), \displaystyle\delta_{\perp}= \displaystyle\alpha\circ(-6\rho+4), \displaystyle\delta_{K}= \displaystyle\alpha\circ(-6\rho+5). $$

Then $\delta_{0},\lambda,\delta_{\perp},\delta_{K}$ are smooth functions defined on $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ with values between $[0,1]$ , and not equal to $0,1$ only on $U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})},U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})},U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})},U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}$ respectively. For an intuitive illustration, please refer to Figure 4.

#### 6.4.5. Gluing of forms

In $U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}$ , define

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{\lambda}=d(\lambda\Phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,+(1-\lambda)\Phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,})=\lambda\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,+(1-\lambda)\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}+d\lambda\wedge(\Phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,-\Phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}). $$

Then by definition of $\lambda,$ it is straightforward to verify that

$$ \displaystyle\phi=\begin{cases}\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,,&\text{on }\overline{U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}}\cup\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}}\cup\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right),\\
\phi_{\lambda},&\text{on }U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})},\\
\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,},&\text{on }\left(B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\setminus U_{\operatorname{gluing}}\right)\cup\overline{U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}},\end{cases} $$

gives a closed smooth $d$ -form when restricted to $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . The reader should now consult Figure 4 for intuition.

#### 6.4.6. Gluing of metrics

In the following, when we write $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ as the input of a differential form, we always mean the unit simple $d$ -vector corresponding to $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ in the base metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,.$ Similarly, when we write $(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\ast}$ , we always mean the unit simple $d$ -vector Riemannian dual to the unit simple $d$ -vector $\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ in the base metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,.$

In $U_{\operatorname{gluing}},$ with respect to the orthogonal decomposition $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi\oplus\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi$ , we can always write uniquely

$$ \displaystyle\phi=(\phi(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi))(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\ast}+\psi, $$

with $\psi$ spanned by covectors in $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi.$ Note that $\psi\equiv 0$ on $U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}.$

By construction,

$$ \displaystyle\phi(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)\equiv 1, $$

on $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ By taking $\epsilon$ in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ small, we can assume that

$$ \displaystyle\phi(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)\geq\frac{1}{2} $$

in $U_{\operatorname{gluing}}.$ Let

$$ \displaystyle K=\binom{d+c}{d}\frac{\operatorname{comass}_{g}\phi|_{U_{\operatorname{gluing}}}}{\inf_{p\in U_{\operatorname{gluing}}}\phi_{p}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)}. $$

We define a Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ defined by:

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{glued}}=\begin{cases}h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,=h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi},&\text{on }\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right),\\
h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K\delta_{K})h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big),&\text{on }\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}},\\
\left((1-\delta_{\perp})+\delta_{\perp}(\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi))\right)^{\frac{2}{d}}\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big),&\text{on }{U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}},\\
(\phi_{\lambda}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big),&\text{on }\overline{U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}},\\
(\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+\delta_{0}K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big),&\text{on }{U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}},\\
h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}=(\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big),&\text{on }B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))\setminus U_{\operatorname{gluing}}.\end{cases} $$

#### Claim 6.4.3.

The metric $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric when restricted to $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ and $\phi$ defined in (6.5) is a calibration form in metric $h$ that calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ .

The reader should consult Figure 4 for intuition.

To verify the above claim, the smoothness of $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ follows directly from the definitions of $\delta_{K},\delta_{\perp},\lambda,\delta_{0}$ in Section 6.4.4 and the definition of $\phi$ in (6.5).

Note that $\phi\equiv\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,,h_{\operatorname{glued}}\equiv h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ on $\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ and $\phi\equiv\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,},h_{\operatorname{glued}}\equiv h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ on $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))\setminus U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ . Thus, by Fact 6.2.2 and Fact 6.3.1, $\phi$ is a calibration and calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with respect to the metric $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ in $\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ and $B_{\delta}(\widecheck{{\operatorname{Reg}\,}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))\setminus U_{\operatorname{gluing}}$ .

On $\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}},$ we have

$$ h_{\operatorname{glued}}=h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K\delta_{K})h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\geq h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}=h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,, $$

as quadratic forms and $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,.$ By bullet (1) in Fact 2.9.1, the form $\phi$ remains a calibration on $\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}}.$ When restricted to $\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right),$ the metrics $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ and $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ are equal to each other. Thus, we deduce that in $\overline{U_{(\frac{5}{6},1)}}$ , the form $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ still calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with respect to $h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$

On ${U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}}$ , first note that $\frac{1}{2}\leq\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)\leq 1$ by (6.6) and Fact 6.2.2. Thus, on ${U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{glued}}= \displaystyle\bigg((1-\delta_{\perp})+\delta_{\perp}(\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi))\bigg)^{\frac{2}{d}}\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\big(\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}}\big)\big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus((1+K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi})\big) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\big(\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}}\big)\big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus(Kh_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi})\big), $$

as quadratic forms. By bullet (1) in Fact 2.9.1, inequality (6.4) of Fact 6.4.1, and (6.7), we deduce that on ${U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}}$ , the form $\phi$ remains a calibration in $h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$ Again, the restrictions of $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ and $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ to $U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ are equal, so $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated by $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ in ${U_{(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5}{6})}}$ .

On $\overline{U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}},$ we have

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{glued}}= \displaystyle(\phi_{\lambda}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\big(\phi_{\lambda}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}}\big)\big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus(Kh_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi})\big), $$

as quadratic forms. By bullet (1) in Fact 2.9.1, inequality (6.4) of Fact 6.4.1, and (6.7), we deduce that on $\overline{U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}}$ , the form $\phi$ is a calibration form in $h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$ Also when restricted to $\overline{U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ , we have $h_{\operatorname{glued}}=h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ , and $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ . This implies that on $\overline{U_{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})}},$ the form $\phi$ calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with respect to $h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$

Finally, on $U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{glued}}= \displaystyle(\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\Big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus\big((1+\delta_{0}K)h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big)\Big) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle(\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}(\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi)^{\frac{2}{d}})\big(h_{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\oplus h_{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\pi}\big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}. $$

as quadratic forms. By bullet (1) of Fact 2.9.1, this means that $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ is a calibration in ${U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}}$ with respect to $h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$ Again, the restrictions of $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ and $h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ to $U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}\cap{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ are equal, so we deduce that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is calibrated by $\phi=\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ in $U_{(0,\frac{1}{3})}$ .

Now extend $h_{\operatorname{glued}}|_{U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}$ to a smooth Riemannian metric defined throughout $M.$ We will still use $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ to denote this extension of $h_{\operatorname{glued}}|_{U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}$ .

#### 6.4.7. Adding a bump to make $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ uniquely calibrated

Use Lemma 2.3.1 to construct a smooth function $\beta$ on $M$ with value between $[0,\frac{1}{2}]$ and

$$ \displaystyle\beta^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\cup\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}. $$

Then in the metric $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ , by bullet (1) of Fact 2.9.1, $\phi$ is still a calibration form. By (6.9), $\phi$ still calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ .

Now suppose $T$ is a homologically non-trivial integral cycle on $M$ that is calibrated by $\phi$ with respect to $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . Since on the complement of $\operatorname{Supp}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\cup\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}$ in $M,$ $\phi$ has comass strictly smaller than $1$ in $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ by (6.9) and bullet (2) in Fact 2.9.1, we deduce that $T$ must be supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\cup\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}$ .

Note that $T$ cannot be supported in $\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}$ , since

$$ H_{d}(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right),\mathbb{Z})=0 $$

yet $[T]\not=0\in H_{d}(M,\mathbb{Z}).$

Now by Fact 5.3.1, we deduce that $T$ restricted to the non-empty closed set $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\cap\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}^{\complement}$ equals an integer multiple $k$ of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\cap\overline{U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)}^{\complement},$ with $k\not=0.$ By Lemma 2.4.1 and the fact that having infinite order tangent to each other is a relatively closed condition, we deduce that $T=kN\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ Since $T$ is calibrated by $\phi,$ from

$$ 0<\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(T)=\phi(T)=k\phi(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)), $$

we deduce that $k>0.$

To sum it up, we have proved that if $T$ is calibrated by $\phi$ , then $T$ is a positive integer multiple of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$

From $H_{d}(U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)),\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ , we can conclude that:

#### Fact 6.4.4.

For integer $k\not=0,$ the integral current $kN\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is the unique integral current calibrated by $\frac{k}{|k|}\phi$ in the homology class $k[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ in the region $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ with respect to the metric $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}.$

#### 6.4.8. Making the metric large away from $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$

This subsubsection is taken from the proof of [59, Theorem 4.1]. By the monotonicity formula for stationary varifolds [1, Section 5.1], there is a constant $A$ such that for any stationary integral current $T$ on $M$ with respect to the metric $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(T|_{B_{r}(p)})\geq Ar^{d}, $$

provided $p\in\operatorname{Supp}T$ and $r<\operatorname{InjRad}M$ . Here by $B_{r}(p)$ we mean the ball of radius $r$ centered at $p$ in the metric $(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ . The symbol $\operatorname{InjRad}M$ denotes the injectivity radius of $M$ . By stationary current we mean that the mass, i.e., area, of $T$ is a critical point with respect to ambient diffeomorphism perturbations that fix $\partial T$ .

By Lemma 5.0.1, there exists $0<\epsilon^{\prime\prime}<\epsilon^{\prime}<\epsilon<\operatorname{InjRad}M$ such that

$$ \displaystyle U_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\subset U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\subset U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)), $$

with the distance between $\partial U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ and $\partial U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ at least $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ , and the distance between $\partial U_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ and $\partial U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ at least $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}.$

Then let $\gamma$ be a smooth function that equals to $1$ on $U_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ and equals to

$$ \displaystyle\max\Bigg\{1,\frac{\sqrt[d]{2\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}}{\sqrt[d]{A}\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}\Bigg\}, $$

on the complement of $U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ , and takes value between $1$ and (6.11) on $U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\setminus U_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$

#### Definition 6.4.5.

Define

$$ \displaystyle h=\gamma^{2}(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}. $$

Then by bullet (1) in Fact 2.9.1, $\phi$ remains a calibration in $h$ and still calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ .

Now let $T$ be an area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to metric $h$ on $M.$ There are two possibilities, either $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is contained in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ , or $\operatorname{Supp}T$ contains a point in the complement of $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . The latter cannot happen. To see this, note that $h$ is a constant multiple of $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ in the complement of $U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)),$ so $T$ restricted to $U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))^{\complement}$ is also a stationary integral current with respect to $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ . Thus, one can apply (6.10) with $p\in U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))^{\complement}\cap\operatorname{Supp}T$ and $r=\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ so that $B_{r}(p)\subset U_{\epsilon^{\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))^{\complement}$ to conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{h}(T) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{h}(T|_{B_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(p)})=\max\Bigg\{1,\frac{\sqrt[d]{2\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}}{\sqrt[d]{A}\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}\Bigg\}^{d}\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(T|_{B_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(p)}) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\max\Bigg\{1,\frac{{2\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}}{{A}(\epsilon^{\prime\prime})^{d}}\Bigg\}A(\epsilon^{\prime\prime})^{d} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\max\{A(\epsilon^{\prime\prime})^{d},2\mathbf{M}_{(1+\beta)h_{\operatorname{glued}}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\max\{A(\epsilon^{\prime\prime})^{d},2\mathbf{M}_{h}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\}. $$

In other words, $T$ has area at least two times that of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in metric $h$ , so $T$ cannot be area-minimizing.

To sum it up, we have the proven the following:

#### Fact 6.4.6.

In the smooth Riemannian metric $h$ (Definition 6.4.5) on $M,$ the smooth form $\phi$ (6.5) on $U_{\epsilon}(B\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ Moreover, any other area-minimizing integral current $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ must have $\operatorname{Supp}T\subset U_{\epsilon}(B\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$

### 6.5. Wrapping up proof of Lemma 6.0.1

Let $T$ be an area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma].$ By Fact 6.4.6, $T$ is supported in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$ However, since $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ is a subset of $M,$ we need to redetermine the relation between $[T]$ and $[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ when restricted to $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$

Since we have $H_{d}(U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))=\mathbb{Z}[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ by Lemma 5.0.1, we deduce that $[T]=k[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ as homology classes in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ with $k\not=0.$ Thus, we have

$$ |k|\mathbf{M}_{h}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=|kN\#\sigma^{s}(C)(\phi)|=|T(\phi)|\leq\mathbf{M}_{h}(T). $$

Since $T$ is area-minimizing in $[\Sigma]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{h}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\geq\mathbf{M}_{h}(T). $$

Thus we must have $k=\pm 1$ and $\mathbf{M}_{h}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=\mathbf{M}_{h}(T).$ This implies that $T$ is calibrated by $\frac{k}{|k|}\phi.$ Now by Fact 6.4.4 and $h\geq h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ , we deduce that $T=\pm N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as claimed.

The bullet in our prompt follows because we have never changed the metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ inside

$$ \hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\cap{U_{\epsilon^{\prime\prime}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))}. $$

Thus, for some ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}>0$ small, in a neighborhood ${U}_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ diffeomorphic to $B_{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ via $\Gamma$ the metric $h$ is the pullback of the standard product metric on $B_{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ .

#### Definition 6.5.1.

For $0<\eta\leq{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},$ we define $U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ , the radius $\eta$ tubular neighborhood of ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C),$ by

$$ \displaystyle U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))=\Gamma^{-1}(B_{\eta}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}). $$

## 7. Orthogonal transverse immersions have persistent singular sets

Now that we have constructed the area-minimizing representative $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in Lemma 6.0.1, we need to choose suitable $C$ and $s$ to create persistent singular sets. As explained in our plan of proof Section 1.1, we have two kinds of singular sets that we want to add, transverse intersections from Fact 1.1.2 and products of $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ with spheres from Fact 1.1.3. Transverse intersections from Fact 1.1.2 contributes a singular set of dimension $(d-c)$ , and products of $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ with spheres from Fact 1.1.3 contributes a singular set of dimension $(d-5)$ .

In this section we will focus on adding the singular sets in Fact 1.1.2.

Now take two copies of $\mathbb{R}^{c},$ with standard coordinate systems $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{c}),$ and $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{c}),$ respectively. Then the product structure of

$$ \mathbb{R}^{2c}=\mathbb{R}^{c}\times\mathbb{R}^{c} $$

gives us a coordinate system

$$ \displaystyle(x,y)=(x_{1},\dots,x_{c},y_{1},\dots,y_{c}) $$

on $\mathbb{R}^{2c}.$

Set $\mathbb{R}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}$ with parameterization $(x,0)$ and $\{0\}^{c}\times\mathbb{R}^{c}$ with parameterization $(0,y).$ In this section we always use

#### Definition 7.0.1.

(In this section only)

$$ \displaystyle C= \displaystyle\,\mathbb{R}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}+\{0\}^{c}\times\mathbb{R}^{c}, \displaystyle\phi_{C}= \displaystyle\,dx_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx_{c}+dy_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dy_{c}, \displaystyle s= \displaystyle\,d-c. $$

By [25, Chapter II, Proposition 7.12], the form $\phi_{C}$ is a calibration form that calibrates $C$ , provided $c\geq 2.$

Our goal in this section is to prove the following lemma:

#### Lemma 7.0.2.

The subset ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)$ of the the singular set of the area-minimizing integral current $N\#\sigma^{d-c}(C)$ obtained in Lemma 6.0.1 is a persistent singular subset (Definition 1.1.1), provided $3\leq c\leq d.$

Before delving into the proof, it is beneficial to review Lawlor’s example in [38, Section 6.4]:

#### Example 7.0.3.

The area-minimizing cone $C=\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}+\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}$ restricted to the unit ball $B_{1}^{6}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{6}$ has a persistent singular set among Euclidean metric perturbations.

More precisely, let $\Psi$ be a smooth self-diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^{6}.$ Then area-minimizing integral currents $T$ with boundary $\partial T=\Psi_{\ast}(\partial(C|_{B_{1}^{6}}))$ decompose into the sum of two minimal $3$ -balls intersecting transversely near the origin, provided $\Psi$ is close to identity map.

Note that above result is totally false if we replace $C$ with $\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\{0\}^{2}+\{0\}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2},$ since White has proved that $2$ dimensional area-minimizing integral currents are generically smooth in [56].

Lawlor’s idea is to construct explicitly an integral current with boundary $\Psi_{\ast}(\partial(C|_{B_{1}^{6}}))$ that is the sum of two minimal $3$ -balls $X$ and $Y$ and prove that the sum $X+Y$ is the unique area-minimizing integral current with boundary $\Psi_{\ast}(\partial(C|_{B_{1}^{6}}))$ using an ingenious calibration argument.

*Figure 5. The retractions and the two wedges*

To explain his ideas, let us start with Lawlor’s calibration of $C=\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}+\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}.$ First, let us define a Lipschitz retraction

$$ \Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}:\mathbb{R}^{6}\to\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}, $$

defined by

$$ \displaystyle{\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}}(x,y)=\bigg(\bigg(\mathbf{g}\bigg(\frac{|y|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg)^{\frac{1}{3}}x,0\bigg). $$

Here $\mathbf{g}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a non-negative Lipschitz function satisfying

$$ \displaystyle\bigg(\mathbf{g}(t)-\frac{t}{3}\mathbf{g}^{\prime}(t)\bigg)^{2}+\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{g}^{\prime}(t)}{3}\bigg)^{2}\leq 1-\frac{1}{16}t^{2}, $$

with $\mathbf{g}(0)=1$ , $\mathbf{g}(t)=0$ for $t\geq t_{3}$ and $\mathbf{g}$ strictly decreasing on $[0,t_{3}],$ with

$$ \displaystyle 0<t_{3}<1. $$

In other words $\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}$ is a Lipschitz retraction of $\mathbb{R}^{6}$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle{\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}}(x,y)\equiv(0,0),\text{ if }\frac{|y|}{|x|}\geq t_{3}. $$

#### Definition 7.0.4.

Define $W_{\theta}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3},\{0\}^{6})$ , the angle $\theta$ wedge neighborhood of $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}$ with vertex $\{0\}^{6}$ as

$$ \displaystyle W_{\theta}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3},\{0\}^{6})=\bigg\{(x,y)\bigg|\frac{|y|}{|x|}\leq\tan\theta\bigg\}. $$

Then (7.4) says that $\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}$ is non-vanishing only in

$$ W_{\arctan t_{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3},\{0\}^{6}). $$

The ODE (7.2) guarantees that $\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}$ is a $3$ -area-non-increasing retraction onto $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}$ , which is defined as follows:

#### Definition 7.0.5.

We say a Lipschitz map $\Pi$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing at $p$ , if the differential ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi$ of $\Pi$ at $p$ maps unit simple $d$ -vectors to simple $d$ -vectors of length at most $1.$ If $\Pi$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing at every point where it is differentiable, then we say $\Pi$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing.

A direct consequence of area-non-increasing property is as follows:

#### Fact 7.0.6.

A Lipschitz retraction $\Pi$ onto a $d$ -dimensional submanifold $N$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing at $p$ if and only if the $d$ -form $\Pi^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N})$ has comass at most $1$ at $p,$ i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{comass}\big(\Pi^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{N})\big)_{p}\leq 1. $$

Furthermore, equality in (7.6) holds if and only if ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi$ maps the unit simple $d$ -vector orthogonal to $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi$ at $p$ to a unit simple $d$ -vector at $\Pi(p).$

Indeed we have a more general fact.

#### Fact 7.0.7.

If we have a smooth calibration form $\psi$ defined on a $d$ -dimensional submanifold $N$ , and a smooth $d$ -area-non-increasing map $\Pi$ onto $N,$ then $\Pi^{\ast}\Psi$ is a calibration form.

The above facts follow directly from the definition of comass, the simpleness of $\operatorname{dvol}_{N}$ and the orthogonal splitting of tangent spaces of the ambient manifold into $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi\oplus\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\Pi.$

From Fact 7.0.6, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}}), $$

is a degree $3$ calibration form with Lipschitz anti-derivative (Definition 2.9.3), since $\operatorname{dvol}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}$ is exact. Direct calculation shows that $\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}})$ is almost continuous (Definition 2.9.3) on $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}$ and calibrates only $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}$ .

Now in the same vein, we can define

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}(x,y)=\bigg(0,\mathbf{g}\bigg(\frac{|y|}{|x|}^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg)y\bigg), $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle{\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}}(x,y)\equiv(0,0),\text{ if }\frac{|x|}{|y|}\geq t_{3}. $$

We can similarly define $W_{\theta}(\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3},\{0\}^{6})$ ,the angle $\theta$ wedge neighborhood of $\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with vertex $\{0\}^{6}$ as

$$ \displaystyle W_{\theta}(\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3},\{0\}^{6})=\bigg\{(x,y)\bigg|\frac{|x|}{|y|}\leq\tan\theta\bigg\}. $$

Then $\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}$ is non-vanishing only in $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3},\{0\}^{6}).$

Again $\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}})$ is a calibration form with Lipschitz anti-derivative and calibrates only $\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}.$

Since the two wedges $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3},\{0\}^{6})$ and $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3},\{0\}^{6})$ only intersect at the origin due to (7.3), by (7.4) and (7.8) we deduce that $\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}$ and $\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}$ patch together Lipschitzly through the region

$$ \displaystyle t_{3}<\frac{|y|}{|x|}<\frac{1}{t_{3}} $$

into a Lipshictz $3$ -area-non-increasing retraction:

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{C}:\mathbb{R}^{6}\to C. $$

The reader should now consult Figure 5 for intuition. Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{C}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{C}=\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}})+\Pi_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}^{\ast}(\operatorname{dvol}_{\{0\}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}), $$

is a calibration form with Lipschitz anti-derivative that calibrates only $C.$

At this point, all of these seem fairly uninteresting and we have just found a very artificial and complicated way to calibrate $C.$ However, a little twist to the above construction immediately proves the statements in Example 7.0.3.

Lawlor’s ingenious idea is as follows. Note that $\partial(C|_{B_{1}^{6}})$ is the sum of two disjoint pieces

$$ \displaystyle S^{2}\times\{0\}^{3}+\{0\}^{3}\times S^{2} $$

By the implicit function theorem of partial differential equations, $\Psi_{\ast}(S^{2}\times\{0\}^{3})$ bounds a minimally embedded $3$ -ball $X$ and $\Psi_{\ast}(\{0\}^{3}\times S^{2})$ bounds a minimally embedded $3$ -ball $Y,$ intersecting at a point

$$ X\cap Y=p $$

near the origin, provided $\Psi$ is close to the identity map.

Now define a retraction $\Pi_{X}$ onto $X$ as follows in the spirit of (7.1) . For any point $q\in\mathbb{R}^{6},$ Use $\pi_{X}(q)$ to denote the nearest distance projection of $q$ to $X$ . On length minimizing geodesic $\gamma\subset X$ from $p$ to $\pi_{X}(q)$ on $X$ there is a unique point,

$$ \mathbf{g}^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\mathbb{R}^{6}}(q,\pi_{X}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X}(q),p)}\bigg)\pi_{X}(q), $$

that is of distance precisely

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{g}^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\mathbb{R}^{6}}(q,\pi_{X}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X}(q),p)}\bigg)\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X}(q),p) $$

to $p.$ Here $\mathbf{d}_{\mathbb{R}^{6}}$ is the distance in $\mathbb{R}^{6}$ and $\mathbf{d}_{X}$ is the Riemannian distance function on $X.$ Now define

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{X}(q)=\mathbf{g}^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\mathbb{R}^{6}}(q,\pi_{X}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X}(q),p)}\bigg)\pi_{X}(q). $$

This gist of this definition is that in a Fermi coordinate chart centered at $p$ and adopted to $X,$

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{X}=\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\{0\}^{3}}. $$

Then again using (7.2), one can prove that $\Pi_{X}$ is a $3$ -area-non-increasing retraction onto $X$ , provided $\Psi$ is close to identity. Thus, we can prove that $\Pi_{X}^{*}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}$ is a calibration form with Lipschitz anti-derivative and calibrates only $X.$

Similarly, one define $\Pi_{Y}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{Y}(q)=\mathbf{g}^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\mathbb{R}^{6}}(q,\pi_{Y}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{Y}(\pi_{Y}(q),p)}\bigg)\pi_{Y}(q), $$

and prove that $\Pi_{Y}$ is $3$ -area-non-increasing. Then $\Pi_{Y}^{*}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is a calibration form with Lipschitz anti-derivative and calibrates only $Y.$

Then again, one can define wedges $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(X,p)$ and $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(Y,p)$ similar to Definition 7.0.4, such that $\Pi_{X}$ is not of constant value $p$ only on $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(X,p)$ and $\Pi_{Y}$ is not of constant value $p$ only on $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(Y,p)$ . Now the two wedges $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(X,p)$ and $W_{\arctan t_{3}}(Y,p)$ do not intersect, provided $\Psi$ is close to identity. This implies that $\Pi_{X}$ patches Lipschitzly onto $\Pi_{Y}$ to give a Lipschitz $3$ -area-non-increasing retraction onto $X+Y$ , and the calibration form

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{X}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y} $$

only calibrates $X+Y.$ This implies that $X+Y$ is the unique area-minimizing integral current with boundary $\Psi_{\ast}(\partial(C|_{B_{1}^{6}}))$ and we get the claims in our Example 7.0.3.

At this point the reader might wonder why the above argument fail in the case of $2$ -dimensional surfaces, since $2$ -dimensional area-minimizing integral currents are generally smooth by [56]. The main reason is that the ODE (7.2) does not have a solution $\mathbf{g}$ with $\mathbf{g}(0)=1$ and $\mathbf{g}(1)=0$ when the number $3$ in the denominators of (7.2) is replaced by the number $2$ . Thus, we cannot patch together $\Pi_{X}$ and $\Pi_{Y}$ as above.

Our proof of Lemma 7.0.2 is precisely a Riemannian version of Lawlor’s arguments. Let $g$ be a smooth metric close enough to $h$ obtained in Lemma 6.0.1. (The closeness of $g$ to $h$ will be determined in the proof.) Our argument will involve five steps:

- (1) With respect to the metric $g$ , determine the structure of area-minimizing integral currents $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ , when restricted to the complement of $U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ (Definition 6.5.1).

- (2) Using the above step, we construct embedded minimal $d$ -dimensional submanifolds $X$ and $Y$ contained in $U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),$ with transverse intersection $S^{s}$ such that $\displaystyle\partial(X+Y)=\partial\bigg(T|_{U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}\bigg).$

- (3) Construct the $d$ -area-non-increasing retractions $\Pi_{X}$ and $\Pi_{Y}$ onto $X$ and $Y$ .

- (4) Prove that $\Pi_{X}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is a calibration form only calibrating $X+Y.$

- (5) Use $H_{d}(U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),\mathbb{Z})=0$ to conclude that $\displaystyle X+Y=T|_{U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}.$

The Step (4) is the hardest and will take up the majority of our efforts. The main difficulty is that we no longer have a Euclidean metric, so that we have to estimate carefully the effects of curvature on our argument. Our proof in this section will start with some preparational work and then go through the above five steps.

### 7.1. Lawlor’s ODE

Lawlor’s ODE in (7.2) will be a crucial ingredient of our proof. In this subsection, we will formally define the Lipschitz functions $\mathbf{g}.$

#### Definition 7.1.1.

For every integer $c\geq 3,$ define a function $\mathbf{g}_{c}(t):[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}(t)=\begin{cases}1-\frac{2c^{2}-9}{8}t^{2},&\text{for }t\in\Big[0,\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2c^{2}-9}}\Big),\\
0,&\text{for }t\in\Big[\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2c^{2}-9}},\infty\Big).\end{cases} $$

We will also denote

$$ \displaystyle t_{c} \displaystyle=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2c^{2}-9}}, \displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{c}(t) \displaystyle={\mathbf{g}_{c}}(t)-\frac{t}{c}{\mathbf{g}_{c}}^{\prime}(t), \displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{c}(t) \displaystyle=\frac{{\mathbf{g}_{c}}^{\prime}(t)}{c}. $$

#### Fact 7.1.2.

The function $\mathbf{g}_{c}$ is a monotone Lipschitz function on $[0,\infty),$ and is strictly monotonically decreasing when restricted to $[0,t_{c}]$ , with $\mathbf{g}_{c}(0)=1,\mathbf{g}_{c}(t_{c})=0$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle 1>t_{c}=\frac{2}{c}+O(c^{-2}). $$

for all $c\geq 3.$

The above fact is obvious. The function $\mathbf{g}_{c}$ satisfies a more general version of Lawlor’s ODE as follows:

#### Lemma 7.1.3.

On the interval $[0,\mathbf{t}_{c}),$ the Lipschitz function satisfies Lawlor’s ODE:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{3}{4}\leq\mathbf{c}_{c}(t)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}(t)^{2}=\left({\mathbf{g}_{c}}(t)-\frac{t}{c}{\mathbf{g}_{c}}^{\prime}(t)\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{{\mathbf{g}_{c}}^{\prime}(t)}{c}\right)^{2}\leq 1-\frac{1}{16}t^{2}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{c}(t)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}(t)^{2}=1\iff t=0. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is a direct calculation. A Mathematica verification will be provided at the end of the manuscript after bibliography. We will give a sketch here. We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{c}(t)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}(t)^{2}=a_{c}\cdot(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}\cdot(t^{2})+1, $$

with

$$ \displaystyle a_{c}=\frac{c^{4}}{16}-\frac{c^{3}}{4}-\frac{5c^{2}}{16}+\frac{81}{16c^{2}}+\frac{9c}{4}-\frac{81}{16c}-\frac{63}{64}=\frac{(c-2)^{2}\left(2c^{2}-9\right)^{2}}{64c^{2}}>0, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle b_{c}=-\frac{c^{2}}{4}+\frac{81}{16c^{2}}+c-\frac{9}{2c}=-\frac{\left(2c^{2}-9\right)\left(2c^{2}-8c+9\right)}{16c^{2}}<0. $$

provided $c\geq 3.$ Now treat the right hand side of equation (7.15) as a quadratic polynomial in variable $\tau=t^{2},$ then the discriminant of the right hand side of (7.15) equals

$$ b_{c}^{2}-4a_{c}=-\frac{\left(2c^{2}-9\right)^{3}\left(6c^{2}-16c+9\right)}{256c^{4}}<0, $$

for $c\geq 3.$ Negative discriminant implies $a_{c}\cdot(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}\cdot(t^{2})+1$ has no root, so $a_{c}>0$ implies that $a_{c}\cdot(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}\cdot(t^{2})+1$ is always positive. The minimum of $a_{c}(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}(t^{2})+1$ is achieved at $t^{2}=\frac{-b_{c}}{2a_{c}}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle a_{c}\cdot(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}\cdot(t^{2})+1 \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle a_{c}\left(\frac{-b_{c}}{2a_{c}}\right)^{2}+b_{c}\left(\frac{-b_{c}}{2a_{c}}\right)+1 \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(2c^{2}-9\right)\left(6c^{2}-16c+9\right)}{16(c-2)^{2}c^{2}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{3}{4}+\frac{(-3+2c)^{2}(-9+4c)}{\left(2c^{2}-9\right)\left(6c^{2}-16c+9\right)} \displaystyle> \displaystyle\frac{3}{4} $$

for all $t\in\mathbb{R}.$ This finishes the proof of the left hand side of (7.13).

On the other hand, when we restrict to $t\in[0,t_{c}),$ we always have $t^{4}<t_{c}^{2}t^{2}.$ Since $a_{c}>0$ due to (7.16), we have

$$ \displaystyle a_{c}\cdot(t^{2})^{2}+b_{c}\cdot(t^{2})+1 \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle a_{c}t_{c}^{2}t^{2}+b_{c}t^{2}+1 \displaystyle= \displaystyle(a_{c}t_{c}^{2}+b_{c})t^{2}+1 \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{9}{16c^{2}}-\frac{1}{8}\right)t^{2}+1 \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 1-\frac{1}{16}t^{2}, $$

provided $c\geq 3.$ This finishes the proof of the right hand side of (7.13).

The claim (7.14) follows from the right hand side of (7.13) and $\mathbf{c}_{c}(0)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}(0)^{2}=1.$

The referee has suggested a more human verifiable approach as follows. Setting $\mathbf{t}=\frac{2c^{2}-9}{4}t^{2},$ then we have $\mathbf{t}\in[0,2)$ . From $\mathbf{c}_{c}^{2}(t)=\left(1-\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{c}\right)\mathbf{t}\right)^{2},\mathbf{s}_{c}(t)^{2}=\frac{2c^{2}-9}{4c^{2}}\mathbf{t}$ , the proof can be done as estimating the range of a quadratic function in $\mathbf{t}$ with domain $[0,2)$ . ∎

### 7.2. Geometric dependence

As Lemma 7.0.2 is essentially a statement about an open subset in the space of Riemannian metrics, we will frequently encounter quantitative estimates or qualitative statements that need a uniform bound depending on the metric. To this end, we give a formal definition as follows.

#### Definition 7.2.1.

Let $X,Y,Z,$ etc., be submanifolds of $M$ . Suppose we have an object $A$ , that is constructed from $X,Y,Z,$ etc., and the ambient metric $h.$ We say the quantity $A$ depends geometrically on $X,Y,Z,$ etc. and $h$ , if the object $A$ varies continuously in its category if we vary $X,Y,Z,$ etc., and the ambient metric $h$ continuously in the smooth topology.

Here by varying $X$ , etc., we mean the following.

#### Definition 7.2.2.

Let $X$ be a compact smooth submanifold of $M.$ We regard $X$ as a point in the space $C^{\infty}(X,M)$ of smooth maps from $X$ to $M.$ Then we say a submanifold $X^{\prime}$ is $\epsilon$ -close to $X$ as a submanifold, if $X^{\prime}$ can be realized as a map in $C^{\infty}(X,M)$ of distance at most $\epsilon$ away to $X$ in the standard metric on $C^{\infty}(X,M)$ .

Here the standard metric on $C^{\infty}(X,M)$ is the one obtained from the countably many $C^{k}$ semi-norms for $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , e.g., [55, Theorem A.4.7].

For instance, the second fundamental form tensor of a submanifold $N$ depends geometrically on $N$ and the ambient metric $h.$ The injectivity radius of $M$ depends geometrically on the ambient metric.

In most cases, geometric dependence of $A$ on $X,Y,Z,$ etc., and $h$ is a straightforward calculation and we will not give a detailed proof.

An easy consequence of geometric dependence is as follows. If a real number $A$ is positive on some $X,Y,Z$ etc., and $h,$ and depends geometrically on $X,Y,Z,$ etc., and $h,$ then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_{h}$ in the space of Riemannian metrics, and $\epsilon>0,\delta>0,$ such that whenever $X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}$ etc., is $\delta$ close to the $X,Y,Z$ in smooth topology and $h^{\prime}\in\Omega_{h}$ then $A\geq\epsilon.$

### 7.3. Normal bundles and neighborhoods

As mentioned when introducing Lawlor’s ideas, we need several geometric constructions, like retractions, wedges, etc. These concepts per se are not limited to minimal submanifolds. Thus, we collect these concepts together in the next several subsections and give the formal definitions. The constructions all depend geometrically on the ambient metric and submanifolds involved.

Unfortunately, our geometric set up will constantly involve three levels of manifolds. We need a submanifold $S^{d-c}$ that are formed by the transverse intersection of two $d$ -dimensional submanifolds $X$ and $Y$ , all of which are again contained in the ambient manifold $M$ . Thus frequently we have to deal with several different notions of normal bundles and neighborhoods. To this end, we give a formal definition.

For a sequence of inclusion of submanifolds

$$ X_{1}\subset X_{2}\subset X_{3}\cdots\subset X_{n}=M, $$

we use $\mathbf{T}X_{j}$ to denote tangent bundle of $X_{j}.$ Then we have a sequence of natural inclusion maps

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{T}X_{1}\subset\mathbf{T}X_{2}\subset\cdots\subset\mathbf{T}M $$

When $X_{i}\subset X_{j}$ , we use

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{T}^{\perp}({X_{i},X_{j}}) $$

to denote the normal bundle of $X_{i}$ as a Riemannian submanifold of $X_{j}.$

We use $\exp^{\perp}_{X_{i},X_{j}}:\mathbf{T}^{\perp}({X_{i},X_{j}})\to X_{j}$ to denote the exponential map of the normal bundle of $X_{i}$ considered as a Riemannian submanifold of $X_{j}$ .

#### Definition 7.3.1.

Define the radius $r$ ball-bundle of $X_{i}$ inside $X_{j}$ as

$$ \displaystyle B_{r}^{\perp}(X_{i},X_{j})=\{(p,v)\,|\,p\in X_{i},v\in\mathbf{T}_{p}X_{j},v\perp\mathbf{T}_{p}X_{i},\left\lVert v\right\rVert\leq r\}\subset\mathbf{T}^{\perp}({X_{i},X_{j}}). $$

If $\exp^{\perp}_{X_{i},X_{j}}$ is injective wherever it is well defined in $B_{r}^{\perp}(X_{i},X_{j})$ , we define the radius $r$ neighborhood of $X_{i}$ inside $X_{j}$ to be

$$ \displaystyle B_{r}(X_{i},X_{j})=\exp^{\perp}_{X_{i},X_{j}}(B_{r}^{\perp}(X_{i},X_{j})). $$

On $B_{r}(X_{i},X_{j})$ we denote the nearest distance projection of $B_{r}(X_{i},X_{j})$ onto $X_{i}$ by $\pi_{X_{i},X_{j}}.$

Note that by definition, $\pi_{X_{i},X_{j}}$ is the composition of the inverse of $\exp^{\perp}_{X_{i},X_{j}}$ with the projection from the normal bundle $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}({X_{i},X_{j}})$ to its base $X_{i}.$

### 7.4. Allard’s regularity theorem

Now that we have set up the basic concepts, it is time to carry out Steps (1) and (2). First recall Lemma 6.0.1, Definition 6.5.1 and Definition 7.2.2.

The following lemma does not need any assumption on $C$ beyond Assumption 4.2.1.

#### Lemma 7.4.1.

If $2[\Sigma]\not=0,$ for any ${{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}>0$ , there is an open subset $\Omega_{h}$ containing $h$ in the space of Riemannian metrics, such that any area-minimizing integral current $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{Supp}T\subset U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)), $$

and $T$ restricted to

$$ \bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement} $$

is a smooth submanifold with boundary and ${{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}$ -close (Definition 7.2.2) to $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ .

If $2[\Sigma]=0,$ replace every $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ above with $\pm N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ i.e., $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ or $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with reverse orientation.

#### Proof.

Let us first deal with the case of $2[\Sigma]\not=0.$ We claim that

#### Claim 7.4.2.

For any $\epsilon^{\prime}>0,$ there is an open set $\Omega_{h}$ containing $h$ in the space of Riemannian metrics such that any area-minimizing integral current $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ is of distance at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ away to $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in the following three senses with respect to our base metric $h$ :

- (1) $T$ and $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as integral currents are at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ away in the Whitney flat distance in the space of currents,

- (2) The induced mass measures of $T$ and $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ are at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ away in the total variation distance in the space of measures,

- (3) The supports $\operatorname{Supp}T$ and $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ are at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ away in Hausdorff distance in the space of closed subsets.

Note that the above claim already implies (7.18).

Suppose the above claim is not true. Then we can find a sequence of Riemannian metrics $h_{j}\to h$ in smooth topology and a sequence of area-minimizing integral currents $T_{j}\in[\Sigma]$ with respect to metric $h_{j}$ that violates at least one of the three $\epsilon^{\prime}$ distance conditions.

Let us first prove that $\{T_{j}\}$ as a sequence in integral currents must converge to $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ . Let $\{T_{j_{k}}\}$ be any subsequence of $\{T_{j}\}$ . By the compactness theorem for integral currents [14, Theorem 4.2.17], we can find a subsequence $\{T_{j_{k_{m}}}\}$ of $\{T_{j_{k}}\}$ such that $\lim_{m\to\infty}T_{j_{k_{m}}}$ exists. Since each $T_{j}$ is area-minimizing and $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is the unique area-minimizing representative of $[\Sigma]$ in $h$ (Lemma 6.0.1, $2[\Sigma]\not=0$ ) we deduce that $\lim_{m\to\infty}T_{j_{k_{m}}}=N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as integral currents by [49, Theorem 34.5]. Now recall the classical fact that if a every subsequence of a sequence has a subsequence that coverges to the the same limit, then the original sequence must converge to the same limit. We deduce that $T_{j}$ converges to $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as integral currents.

Since $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ and each $T_{j}$ are all area-minimizing, [49, Theorem 34.5] also implies that $T_{j}\to N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as their induced mass measures. Finally $\operatorname{Supp}T_{j}$ converge to $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in Hausdorff distance by upper semi-continuity of densities of stationary varifolds [49, Corollary 17.8]. Thus we have arrived at a contradiction.

To prove that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ and $T$ are ${{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}$ -close when restricted to $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ as submanifolds is a classical application of Allard’s regularity theorem [1, Section 8, Regularity Theorem]. We will only give a sketch.

Roughly speaking the core of Allard’s regularity theorem [1, Section 8, Theorem 8.19] is that volume close to balls implies close to balls as submanifolds. Roughly speaking, if the area of a $d$ -dimensional stationary varifold $V$ restricted to a $(d+c)$ -dimensional geodesic ball centered at $p$ on $M$ is at most $\kappa$ off from the area of a standard $d$ -dimensional ball in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ , then the varifold $V$ is $\iota$ close as submanifolds to a $d$ -dimensional standard ball in a neighborhood of $p$ in $M$ .

Precisely speaking, Allard’s regularity theorem implies the following. For any $\iota>0,$ there is $R,\kappa>0,$ such that if we have a $d$ -dimensional stationary varifold $V$ in $M$ with metric $h$ and the area of $V$ inside a radius $R$ geodesic ball centered at $p$ on $M$ is at most $\kappa$ off from the volume of a $d$ -dimensional radius $R$ standard ball in Euclidean space, then in $B_{\frac{1}{2}R}(p)$ on $M$ , $V$ is $\iota$ close as a submanifold (Definition 7.2.2) to the exponentiated image of the tangent plane $P$ to $V$ at $p.$ (Allard’s original theorem is stated with $C^{1,\alpha}$ bounds for varifolds with bounded mean curvature in Euclidean space. However, routine elliptic PDE arguments like [14, Theorem 5.2.15 (7)], upgrades $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates into $C^{k,\alpha_{k}}$ estimate with all $k>0$ .)

Now cover $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ by finitely many radius $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ balls such that none of the balls in the covering intersect ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ . Since $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ is a smooth submanifold, for any $\epsilon^{\prime}>0,$ there is $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}>0$ such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to any of the radius $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ balls in the covering has area at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ off from that of a radius $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ standard $d$ -dimensional ball in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ .

Now since the area-minimizing current $T$ is at most $\epsilon^{\prime}$ away from $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as induced mass measures by Claim 7.4.2, we obtain that $T$ restricted to each radius $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ ball in the covering has area at most $2\epsilon^{\prime}$ off from that of a $d$ -dimensional radius $\epsilon^{\prime\prime}$ standard ball in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ . Now we can apply Allard’s regularity theorem to deduce that $T$ restricted to $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ is ${{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}$ -close to $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $\bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}$ as submanifolds, provided $\epsilon^{\prime}$ is small. By making $\epsilon^{\prime}$ arbitrarily small, we can take ${{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}$ arbitrarily small. We are done.

In the case of $2[\Sigma]=0,$ the above argument still goes through with every $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ replaced by $\pm N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ since by Lemma 6.0.1 the only area-minimizing integral currents in $[\Sigma]$ are $\pm T$ for $2[\Sigma]=0.$ ∎

Now recall Definition 6.5.1.

#### Lemma 7.4.3.

(Candidates $X+Y$ for replacing $T|_{U_{{\eta}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}$ ) If $2[\Sigma]\not=0,$ For any ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}>0$ , and any $0<\eta\leq{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ (Definition 6.5.1) there is an open subset $\Omega_{h}$ containing $h$ in the space of Riemannian metric, such that any area-minimizing integral current $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ satisfies that

where $X,Y$ are smooth compact minimal submanifolds with boundaries $\partial X,\partial Y$ , respectively, and $X,Y$ are supported in $U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ and are ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ -close as submanifolds to the union of

as a submanifold.

The proof of this fact is similar to the proof of Lemma 7.4.1.
