### 7.11. Proving that $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is a calibration

First, let us show that

#### Fact 7.11.1.

$$ \Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y} $$

is a $d$ -form with Lipschitz antiderivative (Definition 2.9.3).

#### Proof.

Since $X$ is a smooth submanifold with boundary, we have $H_{d}(X,\mathbb{Z})=0.$ By the universal coefficient theorem, we have $H^{d}(X,\mathbb{R})=0.$ By de Rham’s theorem, we deduce that $\operatorname{dvol}_{X}$ is an exact form.

Since $\Pi_{X,L}$ is Lipschitz, it is straightforward to verify that $\Pi_{X,L}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}$ is a form with Lipschitz anti-derivative.

Replace $X$ with $Y,$ we deduce that $\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is a form with Lipschitz antiderivative. Thus, the sum $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is also a form with Lipschitz antiderivative. ∎

Next, let us show that

#### Fact 7.11.2.

On $U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ , the form $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y},$ is nonzero only when restricted to interior of

$$ W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(X,L)\cap U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)), $$

and

$$ W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(Y,L)\cap U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)), $$

where it equals $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}$ and $\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ respectively.

#### Proof.

Recall (7.9), we always have $\arctan t_{c}<\frac{\pi}{4}.$ With ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ in Lemma 7.4.3 small enough, we can assume that the intersection angle between $X,Y$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\pi}{2}\geq\Theta(X,Y)>\frac{\frac{\pi}{2}+2\arctan t_{c}}{2}. $$

In our base metric $h$ restricted to $U_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),$ which is just the product of flat metric and standard metric on unit $(d-c)$ -sphere, we have

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(B_{1}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}\times S^{d-c},\{0\}^{2c}\times S^{d-c}) \displaystyle=\exp^{\perp}W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(B_{1}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}\times S^{d-c},\{0\}^{2c}\times S^{d-c}), $$

where $W^{\mathbf{T}}$ is the wedge bundle defined in Definition 7.8.3.

By geometric dependence in Fact 7.8.5, we deduce that with ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ in Lemma 7.4.3 small, we have

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(X,L)\subset W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}+\arctan t_{c}}{2},{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}})}(X,L). $$

Similarly, we have

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(Y,L)\subset W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}+\arctan t_{c}}{2},{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}})}(Y,L). $$

By (7.82), (7.83), (7.81) and Lemma 7.8.4, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(X,L)\cap W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(Y,L)=L. $$

By Definition of $\Pi_{X,L}$ (7.7.2),

$$ \Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}\not=0 $$

only when restricting to in the interior of wedge neighborhoods (Definition 7.7.1)

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(X,L)\cap U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)). $$

Similarly,

$$ \Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}\not=0 $$

only when restricting to in the interior of wedge neighborhoods (Definition 7.7.1)

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(Y,L)\cap U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)). $$

Thus, applying (7.84), we are done. ∎

Now we will arrive at our final conclusion of this subsection.

#### Fact 7.11.3.

$\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ has comass at most $1$ and calibrates only $aX+bY$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$

#### Proof.

In the interior of $W_{(\arctan t_{c},\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2})}(X,L)\cap U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),$ $\Pi_{X,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing by Fact 7.9.12, and sends unit simple $d$ -vectors to unit simple $d$ -vectors only when restricted to $X$ . By Fact 7.0.6, this implies that $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}$ is a calibration form and calibrates only natural number multiples of $X$ by Lemma 5.3.1 applied to the interior of $X.$

Repeating the argument with $X$ replaced by $Y,$ we deduce that $\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is a calibration form and calibrates only integer multiples of $Y.$ ∎

### 7.12. Concluding the proof of Lemma 7.0.2

It is straight forward to verify that $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ is almost continuous (Definition 2.9.3) on $X+Y.$ By $\partial(X+Y)=\partial T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}$ , Fact 7.11.3 and Lemma 2.9.4, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}(X+Y)\leq\mathbf{M}\big(T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}\big). $$

Recall Lemma 7.4.3. Since $H_{d}(U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)),\mathbb{Z})=0,$ we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))^{\complement}}+X+Y $$

is homologous to $T.$

Since $T$ is area-minimizing, we must have $\mathbf{M}(X+Y)\geq\mathbf{M}\big(T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}\big).$ Combined with (7.85), this implies that $\mathbf{M}(X+Y)=\mathbf{M}\big(T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}\big),$ By Lemma 2.9.4, $T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}$ is also calibrated by $\Pi_{X,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{X}+\Pi_{Y,L}^{\ast}\operatorname{dvol}_{Y}$ .

By Fact 7.11.3 and $\partial(T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))})=\partial(X+Y)$ , we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle T|_{U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))}=X+Y. $$

We are done.∎

## 8. $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ cone products give persistent singular sets

Recall from our plan of proof that we will use two type of singular sets in our area-minimizing representative $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in Lemma 6.0.1: transverse intersections from Fact 1.1.2 and products of $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ with spheres in Fact 1.1.3. Our proof of Lemma 7.0.2 in the last section deals with the Fact 1.1.2. In this section we will deal with Fact 1.1.3.

Before stating our goal in this section, it is beneficial to give a definition of $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ . It is well known that the Veronese embedding of $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ is an area-minimizing cone ([33]). However, for reader’s convenience, we produce an explicit smooth calibration of $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ as follows.

Take the standard embedding of the Lie algebra ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ into $3\times 3$ complex matrices, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle{\mathfrak{su}(3)}=\{U\textnormal{ is a }3\times 3\textnormal{ matrix over }\mathbb{C}\,|\,U+U^{\dagger}=0,\textnormal{tr}U=0\}. $$

As a real vector space ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ has dimension $8$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{R}}{\mathfrak{su}(3)}=8. $$

#### Definition 8.0.1.

Define a Riemannian metric $\kappa$ on ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\kappa(v,w)=-\frac{\textnormal{tr}(vw)}{2}. $$

In other words $\kappa$ is $-\frac{1}{12}$ times the Killing form. For the unexperienced reader, we will define the Killing form later in (8.1).

#### Definition 8.0.2.

We will use $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ to denote the subspace in ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ generated by ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}$ below

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}i&0&0\\
0&-i&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\
-1&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\begin{bmatrix}0&i&0\\
i&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix}. $$

The reader can easily verify that ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}$ indeed form an $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ subalgebra of ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}.$

#### Fact 8.0.3.

The $3$ -form

$$ \displaystyle\psi(u,v,w)=\frac{1}{2}\kappa([u,v],w) $$

is a calibration form and calibrates the adjoint action images of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ under ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}.$

The above fact is [51, Theorem 5]. For the convenience of the reader, we will later reproduce the entire proof.

#### Definition 8.0.4.

Define

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}i&0&0\\
0&i&0\\
0&0&-2i\\
\end{bmatrix}. $$

Note that ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ lies on the unit sphere in ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ with respect to the metric $\kappa.$

#### Lemma 8.0.5.

The orbit of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ under adjoint action of ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}$ is an embedded $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ inside the unit sphere $S^{7}$ in ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}.$ The cone $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ over the orbit of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ is calibrated by $\ast\psi.$

Here $\ast$ means the Hodge dual. The experienced reader might identify $\ast\psi$ as the standard $5$ -form in $\operatorname{PSU}(3)$ special holonomy. However, we will never use any connection to the $\operatorname{PSU}(3)$ geometry.

#### Definition 8.0.6.

(In this section only) For $d\geq 5,c\geq 3$ , take the standard isometric embedding of $\mathbb{R}^{8}\cong{\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{c+5}\cong\mathbb{R}^{8}\times\mathbb{R}^{c-3}$ by mapping $x\mapsto(x,\{0\}^{c-3}).$ Then define

$$ \displaystyle C= \displaystyle\textnormal{embedded image of }C(\mathbb{CP}^{2}), \displaystyle\phi_{C}= \displaystyle\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{8}}^{\ast}(\ast\psi). $$

Here $\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{8}}$ is the orthogonal projection from $\mathbb{R}^{c+5}\cong\mathbb{R}^{8}\times\mathbb{R}^{c-3}$ on to the $\mathbb{R}^{8}$ factor. Note $\pi_{\mathbb{R}^{8}}$ is $5$ -area-non-increasing, and by Fact 7.0.7, $\pi^{\ast}_{\mathbb{R}^{8}}(\ast\psi)$ is a smooth calibration form that calibrates $C.$

Our goal in this section is to achieve the following.

#### Lemma 8.0.7.

The subset ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C)$ of the area-minimizing integral current $N\#\sigma^{d-5}(C)$ obtained in Lemma 6.0.1 is a persistent singular subset (Definition 1.1.1), provided $d\geq 5,c\geq 3.$

The proof is actually quite easy. Roughly speaking, recall Lemma 7.4.1. In $U_{{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C)),$ for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in\{0\}^{c+5}\times S^{d-5}$ , the intersection

$$ \displaystyle N\#\sigma^{d-5}(C)\cap\pi_{S^{d-5}}^{-1}(p), $$

gives an integral current $T_{p}$ with boundary $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ and $T_{p}$ is smooth near its boundary. This implies that $T_{p}$ must has an interior singular point, since $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ cannot bound a smooth $5$ -manifold.

Our plan for this section is as follows. First, we will prove Fact 8.0.3 and Lemma 8.0.5. Then we will prove Lemma 8.0.7 using the argument in the previous paragraph.

### 8.1. Proving Fact 8.0.3

For $v,w\in{\mathfrak{su}(3)},\xi\in{\operatorname{SU}(3)}$ define the adjoint action of $\xi$ and $v$ on $w$ by

$$ \displaystyle\textnormal{ad}_{v}(w) \displaystyle=[v,w], \displaystyle\operatorname{Ad}_{\xi}(w) \displaystyle=\xi w\xi^{-1}. $$

where $[\cdot,\cdot]$ is the Lie bracket and all products are taken as matrices.

Define the Killing form on ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ to be

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{B}(v,w)=\textnormal{tr}(\textnormal{ad}_{v}\circ\textnormal{ad}_{w}). $$

It is well known that $\mathbf{B}$ is a negative definite symmetric blinear form on ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ and equals $6$ times the matrix trace of the matrix product of $vw$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{B}(v,w)=6\textnormal{tr}(vw). $$

For instance, this is proved in [18, Proposition 21.24]

The associated $3$ -form to $\mathbf{B}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{B}([u,v],w). $$

Straightforward calculations using Jacobi identity shows that $\mathbf{B}([u,v],w)$ is indeed a constant coefficient $3$ -form on ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}.$ It is also easy to show that $\mathbf{B}([u,v],w)$ is $\operatorname{Ad}$ -invariant.

Thus, the metric $\kappa$ defined in Definition 8.0.1

$$ \displaystyle\kappa(v,w)=-\frac{1}{12}\mathbf{B}(v,w) $$

is indeed a positive definite metric, and the form

$$ \displaystyle\psi(u,v,w)=-\frac{1}{24}\mathbf{B}([u,v],w) $$

is a well-defined $3$ -form.

To prove that $\psi$ calibrates $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ defined in Definition 8.0.2, we can use [51, Theorem 5]. Indeed, just above the statement of [51, Theorem 5] the author explicitly mentions that the calibrated $3$ -planes of $\psi$ corresponds to tangent spaces of $\operatorname{SU}(2)$ subgroups. However, for the readers who are not familiar with the Lie theoretic arguments therein, we provide a completely self-contained proof here, which also sets the proper preliminaries for the proof of Lemma 8.0.5.

Let us first provide an orthonormal basis of ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ .

#### Definition 8.1.1.

Define ${\mathbf{v}}_{1},\dots,{\mathbf{v}}_{8}$ as follows

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}i&0&0\\
0&i&0\\
0&0&-2i\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}i&0&0\\
0&-i&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\
-1&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\begin{bmatrix}0&i&0\\
i&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix}, \displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}_{5}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\\
0&0&0\\
-1&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{6}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&i\\
0&0&0\\
i&0&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{7}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\
0&0&1\\
0&-1&0\\
\end{bmatrix},{\mathbf{v}}_{8}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\
0&0&i\\
0&i&0\\
\end{bmatrix}. $$

Direct calculations can show that ${\mathbf{v}}_{1},\dots,{\mathbf{v}}_{8}$ form an orthonormal basis of ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ with respect ot $\kappa$ . We will also provide Mathematica verifications at then end of the paper.

Next, let us calculate the Lie bracket of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ with the entire basis.

$$ \displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0&0&\sqrt{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{6}&-\sqrt{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{5}&\sqrt{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{8}&-\sqrt{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{7}\\
0&0&2{\mathbf{v}}_{4}&-2{\mathbf{v}}_{3}&{\mathbf{v}}_{6}&-{\mathbf{v}}_{5}&-{\mathbf{v}}_{8}&{\mathbf{v}}_{7}\end{bmatrix} $$

Here the $ij$ -th entry in the matrix means $[{\mathbf{v}}_{i},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}].$

Now we are ready to verify that $\psi$ is a calibration form.

#### Fact 8.1.2.

Any element $v\in{\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ can be sent to a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ by the $\operatorname{Ad}$ -action of ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}.$

#### Proof.

To see this, note that $iv$ is a Hermitian matrix, so $iv$ is unitarily diagonalizable, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle iv=\zeta\Lambda\zeta^{\dagger}, $$

with $\zeta\in\operatorname{U}(3)$ and $\Lambda$ a zero trace real diagonal matrix. This implies that

$$ \displaystyle v=((\det\zeta)^{-\frac{1}{3}}\zeta)(-i\Lambda)((\det\zeta)^{-\frac{1}{3}}\zeta)^{\dagger}, $$

where $(\det\zeta)^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ is any complex root of $\det\zeta.$ Since $((\det\zeta)^{-\frac{1}{3}}\zeta)\in{\operatorname{SU}(3)}$ , and $-i\Lambda$ is a zero trace imaginary diagonal matrix. We are done. ∎

Since $\operatorname{Ad}$ -actions preserve the metric $\kappa$ , to evaluate the comass of $\psi,$ we only have to calculate $\psi(P)$ where $P$ is a $3$ -dimensional vector subspace containing a vector in $\operatorname{span}\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}\}.$ To be precise, set

$$ \displaystyle u=\cos\theta{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+\sin\theta{\mathbf{v}}_{2},\textnormal{ }v=\sum_{3\leq j\leq 8}a_{j}{\mathbf{v}}_{j},\textnormal{ }w=\sum_{3\leq j\leq 8}b_{j}{\mathbf{v}}_{j}, $$

with $u,v,w$ an orthonormal frame of $P$ .

Then by Cauchy-Schwarz, we have

$$ \displaystyle|\psi(u,v,w)|^{2}=\frac{1}{4}\kappa([u,v],w)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{4}\kappa([u,v])^{2}\kappa(w)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}\kappa([u,v])^{2}. $$

On the other hand, by (8.2) we have

$$ \displaystyle\kappa([u,v])^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\kappa\bigg(\sum_{3\leq j\leq 8}a_{j}\big(\cos\theta[{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]+\sin\theta[{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]\big),\sum_{3\leq j\leq 8}a_{j}\big(\cos\theta[{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]+\sin\theta[{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]\big)\bigg)^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle 4\sin^{2}\theta(a_{3}^{2}+a_{4}^{2})+(3\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta)(a_{5}^{2}+a_{6}^{2}+a_{7}^{2}+a_{8}^{2}) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 4\sum_{j=3}^{8}a_{j}^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle 4. $$

Thus, we must have

$$ \displaystyle|\psi(u,v,w)|\leq 1. $$

This shows that $\psi$ has comass at most one.

However, we have

$$ \displaystyle\psi({\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4})=\frac{1}{2}\kappa([{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}],{\mathbf{v}}_{4})=\frac{1}{2}\kappa(2{\mathbf{v}}_{4},{\mathbf{v}}_{4})=1. $$

Thus the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ subalgebra generated by ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}$ is indeed calibrated by $\psi$ .

### 8.2. Proof of Lemma 8.0.5

To determine the orbit of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ under $\operatorname{Ad}$ -action, let us first calculate the stabilizer subgroup of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ in $\operatorname{Ad}$ -action.

Let $\zeta$ be an arbitrary $3\times 3$ matrix. We can write $\zeta$ as a block matrix with $2\times 2,2\times 1,1\times 2,1\times 1$ blocks $E,F,G,H,$ i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\zeta=\begin{bmatrix}E&F\\
G&H\end{bmatrix}. $$

If $\zeta{\mathbf{v}}_{1}\zeta^{-1}={\mathbf{v}}_{1},$ then we have

$$ \displaystyle 0= \displaystyle[\zeta,{\mathbf{v}}_{1}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}E&F\\
G&H\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}iI_{2}&0\\
0&-2i\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}iI_{2}&0\\
0&-2i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}E&F\\
G&H\end{bmatrix} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}0&-\sqrt{3}iF\\
\sqrt{3}iG&0\end{bmatrix}. $$

This implies that $F=0,G=0,$ i.e., $\zeta$ is block diagonal with $2\times 2,1\times 1$ blocks.

Thus, any stabilizer $\zeta$ of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ under $\operatorname{Ad}$ -action of ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}$ consists of special unitary matrices that are $2\times 2,1\times 1$ block diagonal of the form

$$ \displaystyle\zeta=\begin{bmatrix}E&0\\
0&H\end{bmatrix}. $$

Since $\zeta\zeta^{\dagger}=\textnormal{id},$ we deduce that $E\in\operatorname{U}(2)$ and $F\in\operatorname{U}(1).$ Since $\det\zeta=1,$ we deduce that the stabilizer of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ is a subgroup

$$ H=\operatorname{S}(\operatorname{U}(2)\times\operatorname{U}(1)). $$

However, it is well known that $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ as a homogenous space is isometric to ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}/H,$ e.g., [28, p.452 last paragraph].

Thus the orbit of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ under $\operatorname{Ad}$ -action of ${\operatorname{SU}(3)}$ is indeed an embedded $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ in the unit sphere of ${\mathfrak{su}(3)}.$ We will abuse the notations and also use $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ to denote this orbit of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ .

Since both $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ and $\ast\psi$ are $\operatorname{Ad}$ -invariant, to prove $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ is calibrated by $\ast\psi$ , by by bullet (3) of Fact 2.9.1, it suffices to show that the tangent space to $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ at ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ is orthogonal to the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generated by ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}.$

The tangent space to $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ at ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ are generated by ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and vectors of the form $[w,{\mathbf{v}}_{1}]$ with $w\in{\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ , by differentiating $\operatorname{Ad}$ -actions. However, checking (8.2), it is clear to see that both ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and $[w,{\mathbf{v}}_{1}]$ for any $w\in{\mathfrak{su}(3)}$ are always orthogonal to ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}.$ We are done.

### 8.3. Proving Lemma 8.0.7

Recall Lemma 7.4.1. Take an area-minimizing integral current $T\in[\Sigma]$ with respect to a metric $g\in\Omega_{h}.$ Restricted to $U_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C)),$ consider the projection $\pi_{S^{d-5}},$ defined by the orthogonal projection onto the $S^{d-5}$ factor in $B_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}^{c+5}\times S^{d-5}$ . Then by [14, 4.3.6,4.3.13], for $(d-5)$ dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in S^{d-5}$ , the slicing of $T|_{U_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))}$ by $\pi_{S^{d-5}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle T_{p}=\langle T,\pi_{S^{d-5}},p\rangle $$

is a $5$ -dimensional integral current. Intuitively, the reader can just understand this as saying that the intersection of $T|_{U_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))}$ with $\pi_{S^{d-5}}^{-1}(p)$ is a $5$ -dimensional integral current

$$ \displaystyle T_{p}, $$

for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in S^{d-5}.$

Suppose for some $p\in S^{d-5}$ , every point $q$ with

$$ q\in\pi_{S^{d-5}}^{-1}(p)\cap\operatorname{Supp}T|_{U_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))} $$

belongs to the regular set of $T$ . Then since the regular set of $T$ is relatively open, we deduce that there is an open neighborhood $U_{p}$ of $p$ inside $S^{d-5}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{S^{d-5}}^{-1}(U_{p})\cap\operatorname{Supp}T|_{U_{2{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))} $$

belongs to the regular set of $T.$ By Sard’s Theorem ([39, Theorem 6.10]) this implies that for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $q\in U_{p}$ , the current $T_{q}$ is a smooth submanifold with boundary. However, this is impossible.

To see this, by Lemma 7.4.1, $T$ is smooth in

$$ \bigg(U(N\cap N)\cup U_{{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))\bigg)^{\complement}. $$

By Sard’s Theorem ([39, Theorem 6.10]) this implies that $T_{p}$ is smooth in

$$ U_{{{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\operatorname{Allard}}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-5}(C))^{\complement} $$

for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in S^{d-5},$ and such $T_{p}$ necessarily has boundary $\partial T_{p}$ diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{CP}^{2}.$ As $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ cannot be the boundary of a $5$ -manifold [46, page 203], this implies that for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in S^{d-5}$ , the current $T_{p}$ must have a singular set in its interior. We have arrived at a contradiction.

In other words we have proved that $\pi_{S^{d-5}}^{-1}(p)\cap{\operatorname{Sing}}\,T$ has zero dimensional Hausdorff measure at least $1$ for $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost every $p\in S^{d-5}$ . Now integrate this estimate using Eilenberg’s inequality [14, 2.10.25], we deduce that ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,T$ has positive $(d-5)$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure. We are done.

## 9. Conclusions and remarks

Our Theorem 2 clearly follows from Lemma 7.0.2 and Lemma 8.0.7.

### 9.1. About the non-orientable case

Our main theorem Theorem 2 holds if we drop the orientbility hypothesis of $M$ and replace integral homology with mod $2$ homology and integral currents with mod $2$ currents. The proof relies on replacing the gluing calibrations in Section 6 by gluing area-non-increasing retractions. We will pursue the generalizations of Theorem 2 to the non-orientable case in another manuscript.

### 9.2. About singular sets of area-minimizing currents coming from transverse intersections

Using Remark 7.9.1, our proof of Lemma 7.0.2 can be easily used to imply the following fact:

#### Fact 9.2.1.

Let $T$ be the unique $d$ -dimensional area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ on $M^{d+c}$ with respect to a metric $h.$ If $T$ restricted to a smooth open set $U$ equals as an integral current the sum of two smooth minimal submanifolds $X,Y$ intersecting transversely along their interior, then there exists an open subset $\Omega_{h}$ containing $h$ in the space of Riemannian metrics, such that any area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to any metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ decomposes into the sum of two transversely intersecting minimal submanifolds when restricted to $U,$ provided

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\pi}{2}\geq\Theta(X,Y)>2\arctan t_{c}=\frac{4}{c}+O(c^{-2}),\textnormal{ and }d\geq c\geq 3. $$

As mentioned in the previous subsection the condition of the orientability can be dropped if we replace integral currents with mod $2$ currents. Moreover, the sum decomposition $T|_{U}=X+Y$ can be relaxed to the condition that $T|_{U}$ is an immersion with clean intersections, without a sum decomposition or transversality. We will purse it in another manuscript. Here a point in the intersection set is called clean if there is a coordinate chart centered at that point such that the immersion decomposes into two coordinate axis subspaces intersecting along coordinate axis subspaces in the chart.

A hidden point in our argument is that the self-intersection set $N\cap N$ of area-minimizing representative already has some points being transverse intersection, although in general, triple, quadruple intersections, etc., do appear in $N\cap N.$ In case $N\cap N$ is non-empty, why do we still have to add ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)$ manually to our area-minimizing representative?

The reason is that Lawlor’s ideas do not quite work for intersections with multiplicities more than $2.$ At the least the author does not know how to construct the area-non-increasing retractions onto each sheet in the intersection.

### 9.3. About singular sets of area-minimizing currents coming from $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$

Similarly our proof of Lemma 8.0.7 shows that

#### Fact 9.3.1.

Let $T$ be the unique $d$ -dimensional area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ on $M^{d+c}$ with respect to a metric $h.$ If $T$ restricted to a smooth open set equals an $(d-s)$ -dimensional-cone $C(V)$ bundle over a base submanifold of dimension $s,$ then there exists an open subset $\Omega_{h}$ containing $h$ in the space of Riemannian metrics, such that any area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to any metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ has a singular set of positive Hausdorff $s$ -dimensional measure, provided that $V$ belongs to a nontrivial class in the bordism ring.

Here a $(d-s)$ -dimensional-cone $C(V)$ bundle over a base submanifold means a fiber bundle over the base submanifold with each fiber a $C(V).$ Such area-minimizing cones $C(V)$ with non-bounding links $V$ are abundant.

### 9.4. About other spaces of metrics

Our Theorem 2 is proved for the space of smooth Riemannian metrics. Inspecting the proof, it is easy to see that we have only used the continuity of derivatives of the Riemannian metric up to degree $2$ . Thus, our Theorem 2 can be proved as well when we replace the space of smooth metrics in Theorem 2 with the space of $C^{k}$ Riemannian metrics for any $k\geq 2.$

At the other end of differentiability of metrics, if we consider the space of real analytic metrics, then Theorem 2 also holds. To see this, recall the classical fact that real-analytic metrics are dense in the space of smooth metrics. Thus, a non-empty open subset of the space of smooth metrics necessarily gives a non-empty open set in the space of real analytic metrics.

There are also some conjectures about the analogues of Theorem 2 in the space of specially calibrated integral currents in metrics of special holonomy, for example, special Lagrangians on Calabi-Yau manifolds. Our method per se does not yield a way to construct such metrics with special holonomy. However, Fact 9.2.1 and Fact 9.3.1 still apply and it is worth noting both types of singularities in these facts do appear in special Lagrangian tangent cones.
